sunrise-why.title: Why the Sunrise is the most important part of the day
sunrise-why.summary: Established circadian biology plus place-based lifestyle teaching on why first outdoor light is a high-leverage daily signal.

sections.body: Established circadian biology plus place-based lifestyle teaching on why first outdoor light is a high-leverage daily signal.
sections.heading: The big picture

sections.body: Almost every tissue has a molecular clock.  The master pacemaker in the brain (suprachiasmatic nucleus) is reset primarily by light detected in the eye—not by clocks on the wall.
sections.heading: Circadian clocks are light-trained

sections.body: Specialized retinal cells that contain melanopsin project to the circadian system.  They are especially responsive to short-wavelength (blue-enriched) light and to the overall intensity of outdoor daylight.
sections.heading: Non-visual photoreception (melanopsin)

sections.body: Dawn and early morning light have a characteristic intensity ramp and spectral mix as the sun rises.  ” Research on circadian phase shifting emphasizes morning light for advancing clocks and evening light for delay—supporting the habit of front-loading outdoor light and dimming late.
sections.heading: Sunrise as a distinct outdoor cue

sections.body: Dr.  Jack Kruse’s public writing stresses a stronger hierarchy than generic “get morning light”: true outdoor sunrise with an unobstructed solar path (eyes to the horizon disk, no glass) as the day’s primary “solar call,” UV-A/full-spectrum outdoor light as non-substitutable by indoor LEDs, and tight coupling of that signal to mitochondrial redox and the wider light–water–magnetism stack (including DHA in retinal membranes).
sections.heading: Lifestyle-framework note

sections.body: Log the related catalog activity when you complete this habit. Educational only—not medical advice.
